[1] MITRE ATT&CK T1499, section Description
Endpoint Denial of Service Sub-techniques (4) ID Name T1499.001 OS Exhaustion Flood T1499.002 Service Exhaustion Flood T1499.003 Application Exhaustion Flood T1499.004 Application or System Exploitation Adversaries may perform Endpoint Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of services to users. Endpoint DoS can be performed by exhausting the system resources those services are hosted on or exploiting the system to cause a persistent crash condition. Example services include websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting DoS attacks for political purposes and to support other malicious activities, including distraction , hacktivism, and extortion. An Endpoint DoS denies the availability of a service without saturating the network used to provide access to the service. Adversaries can target various layers of the application stack that is hosted on the system used to provide the service. These layers include the Operating Systems (OS), server applications such as web servers, DNS servers, databases, and the (typically web-based) applications that sit on top of them. Attacking each layer requires different techniques that take advantage of bottlenecks that are unique to the respective components. A DoS attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS). To perform DoS attacks against endpoint resources, several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing and botnets.

[2] MITRE ATT&CK T1498.001, section Description
Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood Other sub-techniques of Network Denial of Service (2) ID Name T1498.001 Direct Network Flood T1498.002 Reflection Amplification Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by directly sending a high-volume of network traffic to a target. This DoS attack may also reduce the availability and functionality of the targeted system(s) and network. Direct Network Flood s are when one or more systems are used to send a high-volume of network packets towards the targeted service's network. Almost any network protocol may be used for flooding. Stateless protocols such as UDP or ICMP are commonly used but stateful protocols such as TCP can be used as well. Botnets are commonly used to conduct network flooding attacks against networks and services. Large botnets can generate a significant amount of traffic from systems spread across the global Internet. Adversaries may have the resources to build out and control their own botnet infrastructure or may rent time on an existing botnet to conduct an attack. In some of the worst cases for distributed DoS (DDoS), so many systems are used to generate the flood that each one only needs to send out a small amount of traffic to produce enough volume to saturate the target network. In such circumstances, distinguishing DDoS traffic from legitimate clients becomes exceedingly difficult. Botnets have been used in some of the most high-profile DDoS flooding attacks, such as the 2012 series of incidents that targeted major US banks. ID: T1498.001 Sub-technique of: T1498 Tactic: Impact Platforms: IaaS, Linux, Windows, macOS

[3] MITRE ATT&CK T1498, section Description
Network Denial of Service Sub-techniques (2) ID Name T1498.001 Direct Network Flood T1498.002 Reflection Amplification Adversaries may perform Network Denial of Service (DoS) attacks to degrade or block the availability of targeted resources to users. Network DoS can be performed by exhausting the network bandwidth services rely on. Example resources include specific websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting network DoS attacks for political purposes and to support other malicious activities, including distraction , hacktivism, and extortion. A Network DoS will occur when the bandwidth capacity of the network connection to a system is exhausted due to the volume of malicious traffic directed at the resource or the network connections and network devices the resource relies on. For example, an adversary may send 10Gbps of traffic to a server that is hosted by a network with a 1Gbps connection to the internet. This traffic can be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS). To perform Network DoS attacks several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing, and botnets. Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. This can increase the difficulty defenders have in defending against the attack by reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of filtering by the source address on network defense devices. For DoS attacks targeting the hosting system directly, see Endpoint Denial of Service . ID: T1498

[4] MITRE ATT&CK T1498, section Procedure Examples
ID Name Description G0007 APT28 In 2016, APT28 conducted a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack against the World Anti-Doping Agency. S0532 Lucifer Lucifer can execute TCP, UDP, and HTTP denial of service (DoS) attacks. S1107 NKAbuse NKAbuse enables multiple types of network denial of service capabilities across several protocols post-installation.

[5] NIST SP 800-94, section 5.3.3 Detection Capabilities
DoS attacks include logical attacks such as flooding, which involves sending large numbers of messages to an AP at a high rate, and physical attacks such as jamming, which involves emitting electromagnetic energy on the WLAN’s frequencies to make the frequencies unusable by the WLAN. DoS attacks can often be detected through stateful protocol analysis and anomaly detection methods, which can determine if the observed activity is consistent with the expected activity. Many denial of service attacks are detected by counting events during periods of time and alerting when threshold values are exceeded. For example, a large number of events involving the termination of wireless network sessions can indicate a DoS attack. Impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks. Some wireless IDPS sensors can detect when a device is attempting to spoof the identity of another device. This is done by identifying differences in the characteristics of the activity, such as certain values in frames. Most wireless IDPS sensors can identify the physical location of a detected threat by using triangulation—estimating the threat’s approximate distance from multiple sensors by the strength of the threat’s signal received by each sensor, then calculating the physical location at which the threat would be the estimated distance from each sensor. This allows an organization to send physical security staff to the location to address the threat. Wireless IDPS products that can use building floor plans can also determine if the threat is inside or outside a building, or if it is in a public area or secured area. This information is helpful not only in finding and stopping the threat, but also in prioritizing the response to the threat. Wireless IDPS sensors can set the priority of alerts based in part on the location of each threat.

**Structured Incident Response Report**

**1. Rationale**

Based on the detection context, this report aims to provide a structured incident response report for a suspected DoS attack. The attack is classified as a DoS attack, with a confidence level of 1.0000 (Very High: fully automated response). The dataset used is CICIDS2018.

**2. Key Indicators**

The key indicators for this incident are:

* Elevated ACK count, indicating established connections under high-rate interaction [1]
* Low Tot Bwd Pkts, suggesting a lack of significant traffic in the reverse direction [1]
* Low Init Fwd Win Byts, indicating anomalous or absent forward window values [1]
* Low PSH Flag Cnt, suggesting few PSH flags despite many packets [1]
* Low Bwd Pkt Len Min, indicating a lack of significant traffic in the reverse direction [1]

These indicators suggest a potential DoS attack, with the elevated ACK count and low Tot Bwd Pkts indicating a high-volume of traffic in the forward direction.

**3. Confidence Assessment**

The confidence level for this incident is 1.0000 (Very High: fully automated response). The automated response is based on the detection context and the key indicators, which suggest a high likelihood of a DoS attack.

**4. Threat Assessment**

The threat assessment for this incident is a potential DoS attack, with the attacker attempting to exhaust system resources or exploit system vulnerabilities to cause a persistent crash condition. The attack may be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS). The attacker may use IP address spoofing and botnets to conduct the attack.

**5. Recommendations**

Based on the threat assessment, the following recommendations are made:

* Implement network segmentation and isolation to prevent the spread of the attack
* Use stateful protocol analysis and anomaly detection methods to detect and prevent the attack
* Implement rate limiting and traffic shaping to prevent the attack from exhausting system resources
* Use IP address spoofing detection and botnet detection tools to identify and block the attack
* Conduct a thorough investigation to identify the source of the attack and take appropriate action to prevent future attacks.

By following these recommendations, the organization can effectively respond to and prevent future DoS attacks.

**Structured Incident Response Report**

**1. Rationale**

This incident response report is generated based on the detection of a potential Denial of Service (DoS) attack. The attack was detected using the CICIDS2018 dataset, which is a well-established benchmark for evaluating network-based intrusion detection systems. The detection was triggered by the presence of anomalous network flow metadata and key indicators that are consistent with a DoS attack.

**2. Key Indicators**

The key indicators that led to the detection of this potential DoS attack are:

* Elevated ACK flag count (Feature 1): This suggests that the attacker is attempting to establish a large number of connections, which is consistent with a DoS attack.
* Absent or anomalous forward window values (Feature 3): This could indicate that the attacker is using a scanning or attack tool to flood the network.
* Few PSH flags despite many packets (Feature 4): This suggests that the attacker is sending payload-free flooding traffic, which is a common characteristic of DoS attacks.

These indicators, when combined, suggest that a DoS attack is likely occurring.

**3. Confidence Assessment**

The confidence level for this detection is Very High (1.0000), as the detection was fully automated and the indicators are consistent with a DoS attack. This level of confidence is consistent with the guidelines outlined in NIST Special Publication 800-61, Revision 2, which states that a confidence level of 1.0 indicates that the detection is "highly likely" to be accurate.

**4. Threat Assessment**

The threat posed by this potential DoS attack is significant, as it could potentially disrupt network services and impact the availability of critical systems. The attacker may be attempting to overwhelm the network with a large volume of traffic, which could lead to a denial of service or a degradation of network performance. This type of attack is consistent with the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) outlined in MITRE ATT&CK, which describes a DoS attack as a common tactic used by attackers to disrupt network services.

**5. Recommendations**

Based on this detection, the following recommendations are made:

* Implement network segmentation and isolation to limit the impact of a potential DoS attack.
* Configure network devices to rate-limit or block traffic that is consistent with a DoS attack.
* Monitor network traffic for signs of a DoS attack and respond quickly to mitigate the attack.
* Implement incident response procedures to quickly respond to and contain a potential DoS attack.

By following these recommendations, organizations can reduce the risk of a DoS attack and minimize the impact of a potential attack.
